title: The first ten minutes decide the day

slides.text: The first ten minutes of your day set the frame for the other fourteen hours.
Not because of productivity. Because of self-perception.
Whatever you do first is evidence. Your brain reads it as a statement about who you are.
So make the first thing small and unmistakable: {{first_step}}.
Do that, and by 9am you already have proof. Today, you're {{future_identity}}.

slides.text: Gratitude isn't a nice-to-have. It's a state change.
Naming something specific you're grateful for shifts activity in the brain's reward pathways.
That matters because you can't build a new self-image from a scarcity state.
So start here: {{gratitude_self}}. That's yours. Nobody gave it to you.
Now the rest of the work has somewhere solid to stand.

slides.text: Your self-image is a mental blueprint. It decides what feels possible before you consciously decide anything.
It was built from old experiences — most of them from a version of you that no longer exists.
You will never outperform it. Not with willpower, not with a better plan.
But it isn't fixed. The brain rebuilds the map it uses most.
So use this one: {{future_identity}}.
Read it daily until it stops sounding like a stretch and starts sounding like a fact.

It feels like an observation. It's a habit — a thought you've rehearsed so many times it became automatic.
Rehearsed thoughts strengthen the pathways that carry them. That's all it is: repetition, not truth.
So rehearse the accurate one instead: I am {{future_identity}}, and I have the evidence to prove it.
Say the new line today, every time the old one shows up. That's the whole rewrite.

title: What imagining does to the brain

slides.text: Two groups learned the same five-finger piano sequence over five days.
One group played it. The other only imagined playing it — no keys, no movement.
Brain mapping showed the same region reorganize in both groups.
Imagined practice built real motor cortex change. Not as a metaphor — as a measurement.
Which is why the minutes you spend inside {{dream_scene}} are not time off. They're reps.

title: Replay the day — but edit it

slides.text: Pick one moment from today that didn't go how you wanted.
Watch it back once, plainly. No commentary, no verdict on yourself.
Now run it again — this time as {{future_identity}} would have handled it.
Same room, same people. Different posture, different sentence, different pause before answering.
Run the second version twice more. That's the one your brain keeps.
You just rehearsed for the next time it happens. And there will be a next time.

slides.text: A thermometer reports the temperature. A thermostat decides it.
Your self-image is a thermostat. It has a setting, and it defends that setting.
Go too far above it and you'll self-correct — you'll call it bad luck, or bad timing, or getting ahead of yourself.
Which is why raising the setting matters more than pushing harder against it.
The new setting: {{future_identity}}.
Set it, then let your behaviour drift up to meet it. That direction is the easy one.

title: Every action is a vote

slides.text: Goals are a direction. They're bad at deciding what you do on a Tuesday you didn't sleep well.
Identity decides that. Not "I want to run" — "I'm a runner, and runners run on bad days too."
Each small action is a vote for a type of person. Nothing needs a unanimous result.
You just need the majority. Miss once and the count still holds.
Today's vote: {{daily_habit}}. Cast it, and the identity does the arguing for you.
